text: The hallway light clicked off, and Maya's room went dark and still. Her heart went thump, thump, thump. Pip snuggled close. "The dark is just daytime with its eyes closed," he whispered. Maya took a slow breath and counted the glow stars on her ceiling.

BOOM! The thunder was so loud the windows rattled. Pip hiccupped three golden sparkles all at once. Mom sat on the bed and held Maya's hand. "Thunder is just big clouds bumping into each other," she said. "It can't come inside."

A bright flash of lightning lit up the Pillow Fort. Maya and Pip counted together: one, two, three, four... RUMBLE. "See? The storm is moving farther away," Dad said softly. Every time they counted, the numbers got bigger and the rumbles got smaller.

Maya woke up with wet cheeks. In her dream, a giant shadow had chased her all the way up Moonberry Hill. Dad hugged her tight. "Dreams are pretend pictures your brain makes," he said. "You're right here, safe in your own bed."

In the corner stood a tall, lumpy shape with long, droopy arms. "A monster!" Pip squeaked, hiccupping sparkles everywhere. Maya clicked on her flashlight. It was only Dad's old raincoat hanging on the hook! They laughed so hard Pip rolled right off the pillow.

Grandma's spare room smelled like lavender and old books. The bed felt too big, and the ceiling had cracks Maya didn't know yet. "New rooms are strangers for one night," Grandma said, "and friends by morning." Maya tucked her bunny under her chin.

Outside, the wind howled like a wolf, and a bony tree branch went scritch-scratch on the glass. Maya pulled the blanket over her nose. "That's just the old oak tree waving goodnight," Mom said. Maya waved back, and the scratching didn't seem so spooky anymore.

"What if something is hiding under my bed?" Maya asked. Dad got down on his knees with a flashlight, and they peeked together. There was one lost sock, a broken crayon, and a very dusty puzzle piece. "Nothing scary," Dad said. "Just things that missed you."

The storm made the power go out, and the whole house turned black. Mom lit a candle in a tall glass jar and set it up high on the shelf, far from little hands. The tiny flame danced. "It's like a campfire for our Pillow Fort," Maya whispered.

On the way to the bathroom in the dark, Maya bumped her toe on the door. "Ouch!" There was a tiny scrape and one little dot of blood. Dad stuck on a bandage covered in moons. "Tomorrow we'll leave the hall light on," he said, and kissed her forehead.

The storm had tiptoed away. Rain went pitter-pat on the window, soft as a lullaby. Pip gave one last sleepy hiccup, and a single golden sparkle floated down onto Maya's blanket. "Goodnight, brave Maya," Pip yawned. Her eyes were already closing.
